questions.question: Which of the following statements best distinguishes accumulator‑based architecture from register‑based architecture in the 8085 microprocessor?

options.A: In accumulator‑based architecture only the accumulator can be an operand of arithmetic instructions, while register‑based architecture allows any register as an operand.
options.B: In accumulator‑based architecture the ALU can receive data directly from any register, whereas register‑based architecture restricts ALU inputs to the accumulator only.
options.C: Accumulator‑based architecture stores all I/O data in register B, while register‑based architecture stores I/O data in register A.
options.D: Register‑based architecture does not use an accumulator at all, whereas accumulator‑based architecture has no general‑purpose registers.

questions.explanation:
The context explains that accumulator‑based designs assume the accumulator as an implicit operand and place results there, while register‑based designs allow operands from any register (see pages 2, 93) [Page 2, Page 93].

---

questions.question: In an accumulator‑based microprocessor, what must happen to data read from an input port before it can be used by the CPU?

options.A: It is stored directly into a general‑purpose register.
options.B: It is first placed into the accumulator.
options.C: It bypasses all registers and goes straight to the ALU.
options.D: It is stored in memory and later loaded into the accumulator.

questions.explanation:
The text states that when data is read from an input port it “first moved to accumulator” in an accumulator‑based design [Page 2].

---

questions.question: Which advantage is specifically associated with register‑based architecture according to the provided material?

options.D: Automatic flag updates for every operation.

questions.explanation:
The context lists “The advantage of register based architecture is that extendibility and flexibility in programming” [Page 93].

---

questions.question: According to the description of the 8085 internal architecture, how do registers B, C, D, E, H, and L interact with the ALU?

options.A: They connect directly to the ALU without involving the accumulator.
options.B: They are linked to the ALU through the accumulator and a temporary register.
options.C: They can only hold data for I/O and never participate in arithmetic.
options.D: They operate independently of the ALU and only serve as address registers.

questions.explanation:
The passage notes that these registers “are connected with the ALU through the accumulator and temporary register” [Page 93].

---

questions.question: Which of the following is a disadvantage of register‑based architecture as mentioned in the context?

options.A: Limited number of registers available to the programmer.
options.C: Inability to perform arithmetic directly on registers.
options.D: Lack of support for I/O operations.

questions.explanation:
The text states that “The disadvantage is requirement of complex circuitry” for register‑based designs [Page 93].

---

questions.question: In the 8085 microprocessor, which instruction type modifies the flags but does **not** affect the accumulator’s contents?
questions.explanation:
INR and DCR can be performed on any register or memory and affect flags (except carry) without altering the accumulator, as described in the context [Page 14].

---

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes data flow into the ALU in a register‑based architecture?

options.A: Data can enter only from the accumulator.
options.B: Data must first pass through a temporary register before reaching the ALU.
options.C: Data can enter from any general‑purpose register.
options.D: Data is supplied exclusively by external I/O ports.

questions.explanation:
The passage notes that “Data can enter into the ALU from any registers” in register‑based architecture [Page 93].

---

questions.question: How does the result of an arithmetic operation differ between accumulator‑based and register‑based architectures?

options.A: In accumulator‑based designs the result is stored in a designated general‑purpose register, while in register‑based designs it is stored in memory.
options.B: Accumulator‑based designs place the result in the accumulator; register‑based designs can place the result in any specified register.
options.C: Both architectures always store the result in the accumulator.
options.D: Register‑based designs automatically update all flag registers, whereas accumulator‑based designs do not.

questions.explanation:
The context explains that accumulator‑based instructions “place the result in the accumulator,” whereas register‑based architectures allow operands (and thus results) from any register [Page 14, Page 93].

---

questions.question: Which statement about I/O operations is true for an accumulator‑based microprocessor?

options.A: Both the source and destination registers for I/O can be any general‑purpose register.
options.B: Only the accumulator can be used to hold data before it is sent to an output port.
options.C: I/O data bypasses the accumulator and is written directly to memory.
options.D: The accumulator is used only for arithmetic, not for I/O.

questions.explanation:
The text specifies that “For I/O operation register A only can be used” in accumulator‑based architecture [Page 93].

---

questions.question: Considering the described architectures, which scenario would most likely benefit from a register‑based design?

options.A: A system requiring minimal hardware complexity.
options.B: An application that performs many varied arithmetic operations using different registers without frequent accumulator use.
options.C: A simple calculator that only adds numbers entered via a single input device.
options.D: A microcontroller that only needs to store one byte of temporary data.

questions.explanation: Register‑based architecture provides “extendibility and flexibility in programming” and allows operands from any registers, making it suitable for diverse arithmetic tasks [Page 93].
